meta.title: Who really said "Wine is sunlight, held together by water"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Galileo, at second hand — but not in these words. What is documented is “il vino è un composto d’umore, e di luce,” reported in 1721.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Wine is sunlight, held together by water'?
meta.ogDescription: The saying survives only in Magalotti’s letters of 1721, at two removes from Galileo. The English wording everyone quotes is a modern paraphrase of it.

answer.label: Galileo — reported at second hand, and not in these words
answer.sourceLine: Galileo left nothing like this in writing. The whole basis for the saying is a letter of Lorenzo Magalotti’s, printed in his Lettere scientifiche ed erudite (Florence, 1721), p. 43 ↗: “Mi disse una volta il buon Don Raffaello Magiotti, che il Galileo era usato di dire, che il vino è un composto d’umore, e di luce” — the good Don Raffaello Magiotti once told me that Galileo used to say that wine is a compound of moisture and light. Wikiquote carries that saying, from the same 1721 source, as “Wine is a mixture of moisture and light” ↗. The version in circulation swaps moisture for water and light for sunlight and adds a verb; it is a translator’s improvement on a report of a remark, and nobody has established whose.

source.heading: A remark, reported at two removes

source.excerpt: … io vo dirle cosa in maggior commendazione della vendemmia, e del vino, pure in ordine alle filosofiche contemplazioni. Mi disse una volta il buon Don Raffaello Magiotti, che il Galileo era usato di dire, che il vino è un composto d’umore, e di luce; sicchè ella vede quant’anche, a detta di sì grand’uomo, crescerebbe di condizione il suo gentilissimo trattenimento del fare i vini. E vo dirle il vero, ch’io ho più volte fantasticato sopra questa cosa, per arrivare a intendere quello, che si volesse inferire il Galileo…
trail: Wikiquote gives the saying as “Wine is a mixture of moisture and light” ↗ and cites Magalotti’s letters of 1721 for it — not any work of Galileo’s.

We read the 1721 volume. Page 43, Lettera V ↗ has Magalotti naming his source out loud: Don Raffaello Magiotti told him that Galileo “era usato di dire” it. Magiotti (1597–1656) was a real link to Galileo ↗ — he corresponded with him from Rome and was put forward to him in 1638 as a candidate for the chair of mathematics at Pisa — but he is the only link, and he was reporting speech.

The saying turns up a second time, at p. 15 of Lettera II ↗, where Magalotti asks his correspondent “non si ricord’ella quel ch’era solito dire il Galileo del vino? ch’egli è un composto d’umore, e di luce” — and immediately guesses that Galileo had it from Dante.

That guess checks out as a source for the image, at least. Purgatorio XXV, lines 77–78 ↗: “guarda il calor del sol che si fa vino, / giunto a l’omor che de la vite cola” — look at the sun’s heat, which becomes wine once joined to the moisture that flows from the vine. Magalotti quotes those two lines on the page.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1721 scan, with the long ‘s’ modernised. Magalotti sets the six words he is reporting in italic — vino è un composto d’umore, e di luce — and everything around them is his own prose. He then admits he has puzzled over what Galileo meant by it more than once, which is not how a man writes about a sentence he has in front of him.

sourceLink.text: Magalotti, Lettere scientifiche ed erudite (1721), p. 43, at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Magalotti’s 1721 volume ↗ is long out of copyright and freely readable at the Internet Archive, as is Dante’s text ↗. The English sentence at the top of this page is another matter: it is a loose modern rendering by an unidentified translator, of a date nobody has established, so we assert no rights status for it rather than invent one.

author.name: Galileo Galilei
author.heading: About Galileo Galilei
author.metaLine: 1564–1642 · Italian astronomer, physicist, engineer and polymath
author.bio: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564 and has been called the father of observational astronomy, of classical physics and of the scientific method. He turned a telescope on Jupiter and found moons, argued for the Copernican system in the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632), was condemned for it in 1633 and spent the rest of his life under house arrest, writing the Two New Sciences there. He also, on the evidence of one letter written down a generation later, liked to say that wine was a compound of moisture and light.

cite.sourceCitation: Lorenzo Magalotti, Lettere scientifiche ed erudite (Florence, 1721), 43: “Mi disse una volta il buon Don Raffaello Magiotti, che il Galileo era usato di dire, che il vino è un composto d’umore, e di luce.” The same saying also at p. 15. Reported speech, printed 79 years after Galileo’s death; no work of Galileo’s contains it.

copyAttribution: "Wine is sunlight, held together by water." — Galileo, but not in these words. The only source for the saying is Lorenzo Magalotti, Lettere scientifiche ed erudite (Florence, 1721), p. 43, reporting what Don Raffaello Magiotti told him Galileo "era usato di dire": "il vino è un composto d'umore, e di luce" — wine is a compound of moisture and light. Nothing Galileo wrote contains it, and the English wording is an unattributed modern paraphrase. Traced by Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong words
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quote and Galileo is not the wrong person to put under it. It is a genuine reported saying that has been improved in translation until it stopped being the sentence anybody reported.

items.why: Nothing Galileo wrote contains it, and the seventeenth-century report has him saying wine is un composto d’umore, e di luce ↗ — a compound of moisture and light. “Sunlight” for luce, “water” for umore and “held together by” for composto are all an English writer’s choices, and we could not find out whose.

items.who: Galileo Galilei, as reported by Lorenzo Magalotti in 1721
items.why: Wikiquote gives it as “Wine is a mixture of moisture and light” ↗ on the strength of the same 1721 letters. That much is defensible — a named seventeenth-century informant, in print, saying this is what Galileo used to say. It is also all there is.

A pupil of Castelli in Rome who kept Galileo informed of Roman scientific debate ↗, and the one person Magalotti names. Magalotti was still in his teens when Magiotti died in 1656, so the remark had already travelled a generation before it was written down, and another 65 years before it was printed.

Magalotti himself says Galileo “avealo peravventura imparato dal Poeta maggiore” — had perhaps learned it from the greater poet — and quotes the lines about the sun’s heat becoming wine when joined to the moisture that flows from the vine ↗. Sunlight and moisture were in the picture, in Italian verse, long before Galileo was born.

misattribution.truthLine: Galileo very likely said something close to this, and one seventeenth-century witness says so at p. 43 of Magalotti’s letters ↗. He did not say it in English, and he did not say it in these words.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The remark is doing real work, which is why it survived. Magalotti’s whole letter is about whether light is a substance that can get inside things — he has just been discussing how fire penetrates metal — and a glass of wine is his best case: something that visibly is the summer it grew in. Calling wine a compound of moisture and light is a claim about physics dressed as a toast.

It is also, as Magalotti admits on the page, a puzzle he never solved: he says he has “fantasticato” over it more than once trying to work out what Galileo meant, and had put the question to nobody but Vincenzio Viviani, Galileo’s last pupil. The sentence people repeat today has all of that sanded off. It is prettier and it means less.
detailsBody: The chain is worth laying out because it is the whole case. Galileo died in 1642. Raffaello Magiotti ↗, who corresponded with him from Rome, died in 1656. Lorenzo Magalotti ↗ — born 1637, later secretary of the Accademia del Cimento and author of its Saggi di naturali esperienze — heard the remark from Magiotti and wrote it into a letter. The letters were printed in 1721, nine years after Magalotti’s own death. Every step of that is documented; not one step of it is Galileo writing anything down.

A footnote on how the modern wording travels: Wikiquote’s page on wine ↗ captions a photograph “Wine is sunlight, held together by water. —Galileo Galilei,” with no citation attached, while its page on Galileo ↗ carries only the sourced 1721 form. The same site holds both versions, and only one of them has a source under it. That is roughly how the sentence got everywhere.
context.pull: Il vino è un composto d’umore, e di luce — the six words a witness actually reports.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Galileo Galilei page lists "Wine is a mixture of moisture and light" and sources it to Lorenzo Magalotti's Scientific and Scholarly Letter (1721), not to any work of Galileo's.

Page 43 of Magalotti's Lettere scientifiche ed erudite (Florence, 1721), Lettera V, reads "Mi disse una volta il buon Don Raffaello Magiotti, che il Galileo era usato di dire, che il vino è un composto d'umore, e di luce," with those six words set in italic, followed by Magalotti saying he has repeatedly puzzled over what Galileo meant and had discussed it with nobody but Vincenzio Viviani. Confirmed by reading the page image (running head LETTERA V., page number 43).

Page 15 of the same volume, Lettera II, reads "E poi non si ricord'ella quel ch'era solito dire il Galileo del vino? ch'egli è un composto d'umore, e di luce, e avealo peravventura imparato dal Poeta maggiore," and then quotes two lines of Purgatorio XXV. Confirmed by reading the page image (running head LETTERA II., page number 15).
The Internet Archive holds the complete 1721 scan of Magalotti's Lettere scientifiche ed erudite.
Italian Wikisource's text of Purgatorio, Canto XXV, gives lines 77–78 as "guarda il calor del sol che si fa vino, / giunto a l'omor che de la vite cola."

Wikipedia gives Lorenzo Magalotti's dates as 24 October 1637 to 2 March 1712, describes him as an Italian philosopher, writer, diplomat and poet and a Fellow of the Royal Society, states he became secretary of the Accademia del Cimento, wrote its Saggi di naturali esperienze, and studied mathematics under Vincenzo Viviani.

Wikipedia gives Raffaello Magiotti's dates as 1597–1656, describes him as an Italian astronomer, mathematician and physicist, a pupil of Castelli in Rome who was Castelli's tip to Galileo in 1638 for the chair of Mathematics at Pisa, and who provided Galileo with detailed information on Roman scientific debates and was often in touch with him.
Wikiquote's Wine page opens with an image caption reading "Wine is sunlight, held together by water. —Galileo Galilei," with no citation attached.

Wikipedia gives Galileo Galilei's dates as 15 February 1564 to 8 January 1642 and describes him as an Italian astronomer, physicist, engineer and polymath called the father of observational astronomy, classical physics and the scientific method.
